extracted.intended_audience: novelists and fiction writers (early-to-mid career) interested in craft and producing commercially successful 'breakout' novels
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for writers aiming to make a novel stand out — focusing on setting, character, plot, subplot, voice, theme, and reading-as-research techniques to deepen storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — psychological effect and active relationship to place
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't focus on 'how a place looks but its psychological effect on the characters in your novel'; give your characters 'an active relationship to place' by showing their 'growth (or decline) through their relationships to their various surroundings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use place to reveal character change rather than merely describing scenery. Show how settings influence characters' interior lives and trajectories (growth or decline), making place an active force in the story rather than background decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — larger-than-life, emotionally invested, consequential actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 'larger-than-life characters' who 'act in ways that are unusual, unexpected, dramatic, decisive, full of consequence and are irreversible'; breakout characters also have a 'sense of self-regard. Their emotions matter to them. They do not dismiss what they experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters whose choices carry weight and cannot be undone; make their emotions and self-regard central so readers care. Prioritize bold, surprising, decisive behavior that produces meaningful consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot — complex conflicts, mixed motivations, avoid simplistic binaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for complex conflicts, rather than clear good versus evil; 'consider motivating your main characters in mixed ways. Put them in situations that are strong but in which the right path is not obvious'; remember that 'the hero’s journey is not a universal plot cure' — there are alternate forms that might work better for your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor morally or emotionally ambiguous situations and layered motivations. Avoid relying solely on conventional templates (e.g., hero's journey) — choose plot structures that suit the story's conflicts and the characters' mixed motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot — connect to main plot and combine roles for secondary characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Find nodes of connection where your subplot impacts your main plot; see if you can combine roles for secondary characters, so that they have more than one relationship with your main character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure subplots influence the central narrative rather than existing as isolated diversions. Give secondary characters multiple, overlapping functions to deepen their significance and create structural economy and resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice — free, personal, driven by subconscious truth
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To set your voice free, set your words free. Set your characters free. Most important, set your heart free. It is from the unknowable shadows of your subconscious that your stories will find their drive and from which they will draw their meaning. No one can loan you that or teach you that. Your voice is your self in the story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an authentic, personal voice by trusting emotional and subconscious material. Allow language and character to follow that inner drive rather than conforming to external prescriptions; voice should feel like the author's self in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme — emerge organically from story, not artificially embedded
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If authentic, theme is not something apart from story but something intrinsic to it. It is not embedded, but rather emerges.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let thematic meaning arise from characters' choices, plot consequences, and recurring images or actions rather than tacking on moralizing statements. Theme should be woven into the action and character arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basics first — master foundational craft before advanced techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Basics are important, and writers need to learn those first. (My recommendations if you want to start with the basics: Chuck Wendig’s Damn Fine Story, Janet Burroway’s Writing Fiction, Lisa Cron’s Wired for Story.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure you have solid grounding in fundamentals (structure, scenecraft, point of view, grammar) before attempting higher-level breakout strategies. Use recommended primers to build that foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'bridging conflict' — small tensions to propel scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Maass uses 'bridging conflict,' a tiny bit of tension, to keep readers engaged and moving forward in the story (example: Carson McCullers’s Member of the Wedding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sprinkle incremental tensions or unanswered questions across scenes to maintain momentum. Short, subtle conflicts between beats keep readers invested even during quieter passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and re-read strategically — learn solutions from other books
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading constantly is one of the best (and most enjoyable) things you can do to improve your writing. But re-reading — coming back to books you admire with specific questions — can teach you even more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you face a craft problem, identify authors who solved similar problems and study those passages closely. Re-read with a focused question (e.g., how do they introduce the world?) to learn concrete techniques you can adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding/exposition — introduce setting without drowning readers in detail
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are struggling with how to introduce readers to your fantasy world without drowning them in detail, go to your shelves or local library and see how other authors have solved this problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heavy info-dumps; reveal world details through character interaction, conflict, and necessity. Study exemplary texts for methods of gradual, integrated exposition and emulate approaches that fit your story's tone.
